<description>
Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to
the connection manager. Each job runs on its own thread, shares no state with the node, and
reaches the network only through the Tor proxy: it resolves the chain's DNS seeds, then announces
over BIP324 to recipients on a schedule drawn up front, each connection with fresh isolation
credentials. Nothing a recipient does, and nothing the node sees of the transaction coming back,
changes the plan, and the transaction enters the node's mempool only when it returns from the
network. The old private broadcast connections and relay are removed.

The invariants are specified in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`.

The rest of the tests are in a follow-up to be considered later:
https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup
</description>

I mostly think this PR is way too much work for the value it gets. I seem to be thinking that about a lot of things though.

Looking through my node's logs (long lived ipv4 ip and tor address) over the past few months, I saw 0 private broadcast connections in July, 9 in August (4 didn't send an INV at all, 3 accepted, 1 rejected for insufficient fee, 1 already have), 12 in September (3 didn't send an INV, 2 accepted, 1 rejected for fee, 6 already have), 9 in October so far (4 no INV, 1 accepted, 4 already have). Multiply 3 accepted by 18k listening nodes gives 55k txs/month vs ~20M txs in October so far, so perhaps 0.28% of transaction volume. That usage level doesn't feel like it warrants huge PRs to me.

Could also plausibly just add the hook, and let the implementation live entirely out of tree, with any privacy issues dealt with externally. Then re-merge it, and add wallet support, only once the feature has proven itself robust.

[quoted text omitted]
I think there's three ways you could consider a feature:

 * purely research -- nobody's implemented or using it, people are exploring the idea to see if it works, no real reason not to discuss attacks openly
 * best effort -- this approach gives an improvement on alternatives (just broadcast on clearnet) in the average case, but doesn't really  provide any guarantees against the worst case
 * fully supported -- this is intended to provide guarantees, many people are relying and would be harmed if attacks become more widely known

Personally, I don't think private broadcast should be considered fully supported, and I think the amount of re-thinking it seems to need along with fairly low adoption suggests it could even be more "purely research" than "best effort". I think not talking about the potential attacks probably makes it harder to move towards fully supported rather than easier, as well.

[quoted text omitted]

I'd call that meeting the aims ("improves the privacy of the transaction originator"), even if it's far from perfect or was overhyped ("If the originator sends two otherwise unrelated transactions, they will not be linkable").

[quoted text omitted]
The general pattern is pretty simple. The victim node connects to the attacker both on clearnet and through the private broadcast connection. The attacker correlates the node state on both connections, giving away the privatebroadcasting node's IP address.

Having a non-trivial chance of getting selected for outbound connections costs very little to an attacker. Preventing that a single entity does not occupy all our outbound slots is a design goal of Addrman, but preventing that we don't make a single connection to an attacker with a lot of reachable nodes is not one, nor something we can achieve. Stated differently: it is trivial for today's spies to have the vast majority of Bitcoin nodes connect to them, and then have a non-trivial chance of getting connected to for a private broadcast connection.

_(I'll pass on the terrible incentive for spies to Sybil the network created by the current implementation of this feature.)_

Therefore the only place where we can give meaningful guarantees, is in preventing a private broadcast connection from being correlated with the victim node's connection. This is not something we can guarantee for 2 connections established by the same node, due to the design of our p2p stack, and as i hope the numerous historical correlation vectors and [private broadcast defects](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6449752844) make clear.

I want to emphasize guaranteeing the absence of leaks here. In these discussions i've seen advocates of the current private broadcast architecture challenge critics to lay out the details of specific leaks, so they can be (dismissed or) patched. **This is backwards.** The onus is on advocates of a feature claiming to offer privacy or security, to convince others that it does actually achieve the stated goals under an acceptable threat model. Accepting the feature as secure by default and asking skeptics to keep coming up with end to end exploits to prove otherwise until they get tired of it, is not a serious way to approach development of a privacy feature.

In this instance, this means giving reasonable assurance that state can't be leaked between a regular connection and a private broadcast connection. I'm always happy to consider arguments to the contrary, but as far as i know the only way to get any such assurance currently, is to isolate the private broadcast connections' from the node's state.

I strongly disagree. @andrewtoth @vasild as far as i understand you share this opinion? I think this view underpins much of our disagreement on how to approach private broadcast, so it's important to get some common ground here to be able to make progress.

The status quo before opting into the private broadcast option was to opt into using one of the available tools making a one shot Tor connection to a public broadcast API to obfuscate source+links, or opt into `-onlynet=tor` to obfuscate the source only.

Today, you can opt into the private broadcast option, which sounds like it may protect your source IP, but actually may not if you also run your node on clearnet. And despite marking it as experimental, some users may consider it relatively more reliable than an external tool maintained by a single person, because it was released by Bitcoin Core :tm:. Others may switch to using it with *some* expectation of privacy ("surely the Core developers wouldn't release a privacy feature which can be defeated *that* easily, they are just being overly conservative in marking it as experimental").

In both cases, this gives users a false sense of security, which i think ranks pretty high in the list of things Bitcoin Core should be very careful not to do.

Now you may argue there exists some users with a desire for privacy that would neither use the one-shot Tor broadcast tools, nor the `onlynet=tor` option, but would use `-privatebroadcast` AND would not change their behaviour due to thinking they are now private (which falls under the footgun discussed just above). And you may say these users were previously susceptible to existing spies on clearnet, so `-privatebroadcast` is an improvement for them.

That may be true before the spies adapt (which is a tautology in itself: users are secure if nobody cares to attack them), but actually makes things even worse once they do. Now the spy can still deanonymize transactions, but they also Sybil the network and we give them for free a "transactions made by users with a particular desire for privacy" filter!

Therefore, i think we should stop describe the current implementation of this feature a "best effort". It’s an innocuous footgun at best, until people start using it and spies adapt, at which point it becomes actively harmful. I understand this would not be true if we fixed all possible leaks, but i think this PR is the only way to get reasonable assurance about this.

[2026-10-28] c:6476783810 comment by andrewtoth (member):
To be perfectly clear I believe separating the node state as much as possible from private broadcast is the correct goal. However, I shared some concerns about this approach in an earlier draft here https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/pull/7#issuecomment-6201251786, and the same concerns were raised independently by vasild here https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36628#issuecomment-6413061893. I don't think using the built-in DNS seeds to source addresses for private broadcast is the right approach, and I don't think we should drop i2p or direct tor onion connections.

The latter concern doesn't seem to continue to make sense if we successfully execute separating the rest of the state.

Regarding the former concern: as of today that would require us to continue using addrman. Since this is an experimental feature, I don't think we need to rush to a solution. I don't think this needs to be done by v33, and we can brainstorm for other ways to better source addresses. IMO supplying addresses is also a better interface for a tool, since other consumers could source addresses how they wish (say just give the tool mempool.space's node IPs) without dependence on the built-in seeds.

Are these two tradeoffs acceptable, while taking the rest of the patch? I'm not sure. I understand the security team needs to use discretion when discussing possible vulnerabilities, but the status quo here is quite frustrating I'm sure for both sides. How can we know if the issue with only addrman or tor onions or i2p are realistically exploitable?

I think the status quo for most users is just using default broadcast, and everyone desires privacy (but they don't know they desire it until someone reveals to them they've violated it). I think making even the current version default behavior if we detect access to a privacy network (and warning if we can't) would be a vast improvement over the status quo. So I think improving the UX of private broadcast (by adding it to wallet, package relay, synchronous, etc.) on the way to making it default behavior is the correct path forward. That way a sybil attacker will spend a lot more resources to find out transactions that are just the default.

Of course we should continue to harden the privacy against these attacks as well, but I don't think the status quo makes this feature less valuable or somehow dangerous to users.
